newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danisco sees EU enlargement good for sugar.
newsitem.headline: Danisco sees EU enlargement good for sugar.

text.p: Danish sugar producer Danisco's president, Mogens Granborg, said on Monday that plans to enlarge the European Union from its current 15 members to a possible 25 states would benefit sugar traders and producers.

In a speech to the World Sugar Farmers' Conference in the Danish capital on Monday he said that Danisco, the only sugar producer in Denmark and Sweden, gained experience of eastern European conditions in the integration into the EU of eight factories in former East Germany which it has merged into one.
"There is no reason to delay the political and economic process that will result in a united Europe with 25 member states," Granborg said.

"In the sugar balance the enlargement of the EU will not be of great importance, but production methods, yields and trade will be favourably influenced by the enlargement and we are prepared to accept the challenges implied on our own sugar production," he said.

He added that Danisco, the fourth largest sugar producer in Europe, wished to play a role in developing the sugar sector in one or preferably more of the eastern European countries expected to join the EU. He gave no details.
Danisco increased total production to just over one million tonnes of sugar in 1996, from 922,000 the year before.
The bulk of the 1996 production came from its Danish operation, with 503,000 tonnes. Sweden's contribution was 397, tonnes and its German plant produced 146,000 tonnes.
Granborg said that Danisco planned to reduce the number of its plants in Denmark and Sweden in the year 2000 without reducing production.
He added that Danisco, a beet grower in its home region, could achieve future growth through cane.

"Danisco is an expansive group with activities in foods, packaging and food ingredients on all continents except Africa and we therefore think that our future expansion within sugar could just as naturally be based on sugar cane as sugar beet," he told conference delegates.

He said that his company was researching into genetic manipulation of sugar beet seed to produce a plant resistant to disease and to RoundUp herbicide and expected to have a product on the market in three to five years. --Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650
